paper_name: Operations Management and Strategic Management (Strategic Management)
author: Ranjith Shivahari
title: Porter's
simple_words: Five pressures decide how profitable an industry is. Find which force is strong and plan around it.

definitions.meaning: A model to analyse industry structure and its attractiveness through five competitive forces that shape long-run profit.
Products from a different industry that meet the same customer need, e.g. tea for coffee, rail for air travel.

key_points: The ==five forces== are: new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, substitutes, rivalry.
Stronger forces mean lower industry profit; weaker forces mean higher profit.
High entry barriers (e.g. licensing, scale) reduce the threat of new entrants.
!!Rivalry is among firms in the same industry; substitutes come from other industries.!!

rows: Few big buyers, easy to switch

insight.punchline: Match the situation to the force!
insight.text: Read the case, ask who is pressing on profit, then name that one force.

memory_trick.explanation: Picture your shop: newcomers want to open, sellers supply you, buyers bargain, other ways to meet the same need (substitutes) pull customers, rival shops around you compete.

steps: Read the situation in the case
Ask who is pressing on profit
Say strong or weak, with reason
exam_tip: Same-industry look-alike rivals point to rivalry. A different-industry product meeting the same need points to substitutes.

doubt.question: Are government and technology also forces?
doubt.answer: No. Porter's model has exactly five forces. Government and technology matter through their effect on the five (e.g. regulation raising entry barriers); wider macro factors are in PESTEL.

mistakes.wrong: Listing government as the sixth force
mistakes.right: Porter has five forces; government acts through them, e.g. licensing raises entry barriers.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a rival brand in the same industry a substitute
mistakes.right: Same-industry competitors are rivalry; substitutes come from a different industry meeting the same need.

mistakes.wrong: Applying the model to one firm's internal strengths
mistakes.right: It analyses the industry; internal strengths and weaknesses belong to other tools such as SWOT.

reviewer_note: Corrected per examiner feedback: tip, memory trick wording and doubt answer revised.
check_notes: Writer: Corrected per examiner feedback: tip, memory trick wording and doubt answer revised.

Checker 1: Definition 2 example (tea for coffee): the note defines substitutes strictly as products from a different industry. Tea and coffee are often grouped in the same hot-beverages industry, so this example could confuse students about that rule. A safer cross-industry example would be 'video conferencing for business air travel' or 'e-mail for courier service'. Keep 'rail for air travel'.
